t: Minimum Cost to Connect Two Groups of Points: Bitmask DP
o:
## Understanding the problem

We must choose edges between the two groups so that every point on **both** sides touches at least one chosen edge (extra edges are allowed but cost money), paying the least possible total. Multi-edges between the same pair never help, so the search space is effectively subsets of the size1 x size2 cost grid.

**Example 1:** cost = [[15, 96], [36, 2]]. Edges 1-A (15) and 2-B (2) cover everyone for 17; any other combination costs more.

**Example 2:** cost = [[1, 3, 5], [4, 1, 1], [1, 5, 3]]. Edges 1-A, 2-B, 2-C, 3-A cost 1+1+1+1 = 4. Note that point 2 of group 1 and point A both have degree 2, which is perfectly legal - only coverage matters.

**Example 3** confirms answers are not just per-row minima: sometimes a row must buy expensive edges so columns get covered cheaply overall.

The decisive constraint is size1, size2 <= 12: a bitmask over the 4096 subsets of group 2 is clearly intended, pointing at exponential-in-n dynamic programming rather than polynomial matching machinery.
k: Each row of group 1 needs at least one edge, and every column of group 2 must appear in at least one chosen edge; anything beyond that is waste.

An optimal solution always exists where each row contributes exactly one primary edge; leftover columns are then covered by their globally cheapest edge, which is always attachable because every row already has an edge.
size2 <= 12 makes subsets of group 2 a viable DP state: there are at most 4096 of them.

a.n: Approach 1: Memoized Enumeration of Row Subsets
a.i: Process rows one at a time, deciding what each row connects to. From state (row index, bitmask of covered columns) a row either takes exactly one column of its choice - possibly an already-covered one, since every row needs an edge - or grabs two or more not-yet-covered columns at once. Enumerating those choices exhaustively is obviously correct; memoization keeps the state count at m * 2^n.
s: Define dfs(i, mask): minimum cost for rows i.. given the set mask of covered columns.
Base case i == m: return 0 if mask covers all columns, otherwise infinity.
For row i, try every single column j: pay cost[i][j] and recurse with mask | (1 << j).
Additionally try every submask s of uncovered columns with popcount >= 2: pay sum of cost[i][j] over j in s and recurse with mask | s.
a.t: O(m * 3^n) - summed over all masks, each row enumerates 3^n (mask, submask) pairs, plus O(n) single-column moves per state.

a.n: Approach 2: One Primary Edge per Row + Greedy Completion (Optimal)
a.i: Shrink the branching: let each row pick exactly one column, then finish by handing every still-uncovered column its cheapest edge over all rows. This is safe precisely because every row must have an edge anyway - the global minimum edge into any column can always be attached at the end without breaking degree requirements. The DP state collapses to dp[mask], with a single O(n) fan-out per state per row.
s: Precompute minCol[j] = minimum of cost[i][j] over all rows i.
Initialize dp[0] = 0: no rows processed, nothing covered.
For each row i and each reachable mask, try attaching row i to every column j: relax dpNext[mask | 1<<j] with dp[mask] + cost[i][j].
After all rows, answer = min over masks of dp[mask] plus sum of minCol[j] for uncovered columns j.
a.t: O(m * n * 2^n) - three nested loops over rows, masks, and columns (~600K relaxations at n = 12).
a.sp: O(2^n) - two rolling arrays indexed by mask.

w:
Lead with Approach 2 - it is the intended solution, and the greedy-completion argument is the part worth articulating clearly. Fall back to Approach 1 if you cannot convince yourself of the reduction; it is still fast enough at n <= 12.

**Pitfalls.** Forcing a perfect matching where each column is used once - wrong, columns may absorb many edges; forgetting the completion term for uncovered columns; assuming a row may stay unconnected if its edges are expensive.

**Follow-ups.** Handle size1 < size2 by swapping groups or transposing; recover the actual edge set via predecessor bookkeeping; count the number of distinct optimal solutions.
